Then I thought it would be funny to give him a variation of the Trolley problem. I told him some bomb hit would Japan and get everyone there, but God gave him the option of directing the bomb elsewhere. I told him his friends and family were in Japan, and so he said he'd direct the bomb elsewhere. But then I told him the people elsewhere had families too, and asked him how he would feel if his friends died. Did he really want to inflict that pain on others? He kind of shut down for a bit, and then decided that he didn't want any part in the bombing, and that he would choose not to choose. But then I told him that he was letting everyone on Japan die, when he had the option of saving them. Then the guy tried to get out of it by saying he'd evacuate everyone, or let the women and children go, etc. I shot him down with "you can't do that" for all of them, and he really agonized over the dilemma. It was amusing and touching.

So this seemed like a pretty nice guy, and my impression of him was a good one. I ended up chatting with him when I had the chance.

To choose not to choose, should the bomb be headed down no matter what you did, and instead try to save whatever lives you could, is the strongest moral choice.
